subject: history

moments.title: Birmingham to Selma
moments.who: Martin Luther King Jr. and SCLC
moments.body: Birmingham campaign (April-May 1963): Bull Connor's dogs and fire hoses on children televised globally. King jailed; writes 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'. Mississippi Freedom Summer (1964). March from Selma to Montgomery (March 1965): Bloody Sunday on Edmund Pettus Bridge (7 March) leads directly to the Voting Rights Act (6 August 1965).

quote.text: I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed.
quote.attrib: Martin Luther King Jr., March on Washington, 28 August 1963

moments.takeaway: King's strategy: provoke televised confrontations that exposed the moral character of segregation to the national audience.

moments.title: Malcolm X breaks from Nation of Islam
moments.body: March 1964: Malcolm X leaves the Nation of Islam after disputes with Elijah Muhammad. Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca (April 1964) shifts his view of race. He founds the Organisation of Afro-American Unity. 21 February 1965: assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom, Harlem.
moments.takeaway: Malcolm X's 'by any means necessary' contrasted with King's nonviolence. Both were murdered. The Autobiography (1965, with Alex Haley) shaped Black political consciousness for generations.

moments.title: King assassinated
moments.body: 4 April 1968: King is shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel, Memphis, where he had come to support striking sanitation workers. James Earl Ray pleads guilty (1969). Riots follow in over 100 US cities. The Fair Housing Act passes a week later.
moments.takeaway: King was 39. His Poor People's Campaign (his planned next phase, expanding from civil rights to economic justice) was cut short.

now.title: After the movement
now.body: The Voting Rights Act was weakened by Shelby County v. Holder (2013). Mass incarceration (Michelle Alexander, 'The New Jim Crow', 2010) is read by many as new segregation. Black Lives Matter (since 2013) revived street activism. The MLK federal holiday (since 1986) coexists with continuing debates over reparations and structural racism.
now.open_questions: Did the movement succeed? Legal segregation ended; economic and political inequality persist. Different metrics give different answers.

reflection: The Civil Rights Movement remade American law in a decade — and exposed how much of inequality was structural beyond what law alone could fix. The dialogue between King's integrationist nonviolence and Malcolm X's Black nationalism still shapes how Americans think about race and justice.
